\section[nublado]{nublado — cloudy, overcast}

\label{lesson:ES-C698-nublado}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the drizzle, then the Spanish for to drizzle.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: nublado}
\textbf{nublado} — \textquotedblleft{}cloudy, overcast\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Hoy está nublado.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{It is cloudy today.}
\end{quote}

Used with \emph{estar}: \emph{está nublado}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{nublado} is built on \emph{nublo} \textquotedblleft{}cloud\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{nūbilus} \textquotedblleft{}cloudy\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{nūbēs} \textquotedblleft{}cloud\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nublado}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nublado}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{nublado}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the drizzle, then the Spanish for to drizzle, then say \emph{nublado} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does nublado mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Cloudy, overcast\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[despejado]{despejado — clear (sky); awake, alert}

\label{lesson:ES-C698-despejado}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to drizzle, then the Spanish for cloudy.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: despejado}
\textbf{despejado} — \textquotedblleft{}clear (sky); awake, alert\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mañana el cielo estará despejado.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Tomorrow the sky will be clear.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Una noche despejada} — a clear night.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{despejado} is the past form of \emph{despejar} \textquotedblleft{}to clear\textquotedblright{}, which came from Portuguese \emph{despejar} (EtymDB), built on \emph{des-} and a verb meaning \textquotedblleft{}to hinder\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[soleado]{soleado — sunny}

\label{lesson:ES-C698-soleado}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for cloudy, then the Spanish for clear.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: soleado}
\textbf{soleado} — \textquotedblleft{}sunny\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Fue un día soleado y tranquilo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{It was a sunny, quiet day.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Hace sol} is the everyday way to say it is sunny.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{soleado} is built on \emph{sol} \textquotedblleft{}sun\textquotedblright{}, which is inherited from Latin \emph{sōl} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[nublarse]{nublarse — to cloud over}

\label{lesson:ES-C698-nublarse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for clear, then the Spanish for sunny.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: nublarse}
\textbf{nublarse} — \textquotedblleft{}to cloud over\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Por la tarde se nubló.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{It clouded over in the afternoon.}
\end{quote}

Also of the eyes or the mind: \emph{se le nubló la vista}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{nublarse} comes from Latin \emph{nūbilāre} \textquotedblleft{}to be cloudy\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built on \emph{nūbilus} \textquotedblleft{}cloudy\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{nūbēs} \textquotedblleft{}cloud\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[despejar]{despejar — to clear (up); to clear (a space)}

\label{lesson:ES-C698-despejar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for sunny, then the Spanish for to cloud over.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: despejar}
\textbf{despejar} — \textquotedblleft{}to clear (up); to clear (a space)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Después de la lluvia despejó.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{After the rain it cleared up.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Despejar la mesa} — to clear the dishes away.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{despejar} came from Portuguese \emph{despejar} (EtymDB), built on \emph{des-} and \emph{pejar} \textquotedblleft{}to hinder\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{pedica} \textquotedblleft{}a fetter for the feet\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
